name: journal-did-paul-reach-spain.json
content:
Did Paul ever reach Spain? He meant to. He told the church at Rome that he would visit them on his way there. Acts, the only narrative of his travels, ends in Rome with no word of Spain, and the first writer who may say he went there wrote about thirty years after his death, in a phrase that names no country.

The [paulus_link slug="paul-in-prison" /] entry left Paul under guard in Rome. This one asks whether he ever left.

The plan in Romans

Paul wrote Romans from Corinth, before his last voyage to Jerusalem. He says he has preached the gospel from Jerusalem all the way round to Illyricum, and that his rule is to go where Christ has not been named, so that he does not build on another man's foundation.1 There is no room left for him in those regions, he says. So he hopes to see the Romans in passing on his way to Spain, and to be sent on from there with their help.2

First, though, he has to take the money he has collected to Jerusalem. When that is done, he writes, he will set out by way of Rome for Spain.3

That is the whole of Paul's own evidence: a plan, stated twice in one chapter. It shows his view of Rome as well. The church there was founded by someone else, so Rome was a stop on the way and the work lay further west. Spain was the far end of the Roman world for a man travelling from the east. Gades, the modern Cádiz, stood on the Atlantic beyond the straits.

What Acts says

Acts says nothing. Paul goes to Jerusalem, is arrested, spends two years in custody at Caesarea, appeals to Caesar and is shipped to Rome. The book ends with him living two whole years there at his own expense, under guard, welcoming visitors and preaching without hindrance.4 There is no trial and no release.

Luke may hint at the end he knew. Paul tells the elders of Ephesus that none of them will see his face again, and they weep because of it.5 Many readers take that as Luke's way of telling us that Paul never came back east. It says nothing about Spain either way. [paulus_link slug="a-death-the-scriptures-never-record" /] sets out what the sources say about how Paul died.

The later witnesses

The earliest witness outside the New Testament is the letter of the church of Rome to Corinth that we call 1 Clement, usually dated to the 90s. It says that Paul, after being seven times in chains, exiled and stoned, and after preaching in the East and in the West, "having taught righteousness unto the whole world and having reached the farthest bounds of the West", bore his testimony before the rulers and departed from the world.6

"The farthest bounds of the West" is the strongest line for Spain. A Greek writer could use it of the Atlantic edge of Europe. But the letter was written to Corinth, and from the eastern side of the sea Rome itself was the west. Clement does not name Spain. He may mean it, or he may mean Rome, where he goes on to place Paul's testimony before the rulers.

The first text to name Spain is the Muratorian fragment, a Latin list of the books read in the church. It says Luke left out of Acts "the departure of Paul from the city as he set out for Spain".7 The fragment is usually dated to the late second century, though Geoffrey Hahneman argued for the fourth.8 Either way it comes a century or more after Paul.

The Acts of Peter, a second-century romance, opens with Paul leaving Rome for Spain after a vision, with the believers walking him to the harbour.9 Eusebius, writing in the early fourth century, reports a tradition that Paul was freed after his first defence, went out again to preach, and came to Rome a second time to die.10 He does not name Spain either.

[paulus_link slug="chronology" /] gives the dates on which each of these depends, and [paulus_link slug="pauls-missionary-journeys" /] maps the travels Acts does record.

How I read it

Paul planned to go. No source from his own century says plainly that he went. The first source that names Spain is a list written about a hundred years later, and it reads like an inference from Romans 15. I know of no early Spanish church that named Paul as its founder, and no letter of his goes to Spain or names a convert there.

So the honest answer is that we do not know, and that the evidence leans against it. I hold the question open, because 1 Clement can be read the other way, and a reader who takes "the farthest bounds of the West" as Spain has a case.

There is a lesson in it for any believer. Paul announced a voyage and the record does not show that it happened. The Qur'an tells the believer never to say of anything, "I will do that tomorrow," without adding, "If Allah wills."11 Every person's plans stand under God's will, an apostle's as much as anyone's. Allāhu aʿlam.

Did Paul go to Spain? Questions readers ask

Did Paul plan to go to Spain?

Yes. He told the Romans he would visit them on his way to Spain (Romans 15:24, 28).

Does the Bible say Paul went to Spain?

No. Acts ends with Paul under guard in Rome for two years (Acts 28:30–31), and no New Testament book records a voyage to Spain.

What is the earliest evidence that Paul reached Spain?

1 Clement 5, from the 90s, says he reached "the farthest bounds of the West" without naming a country. The Muratorian fragment, later still, is the first text to name Spain.

Was Paul released from his Roman imprisonment?

Eusebius reports a tradition that he was, and that he came back to Rome later to die (Ecclesiastical History 2.22). Acts does not say.
